info.name: machxi API
info.description:
Smoke and documentation collection for the machxi API (ADR-0021).

Run it top to bottom — with the Collection Runner or `pnpm test:postman` —
against a local stack (`pnpm docker:up && pnpm db:setup && pnpm db:seed -- --dev`
and `pnpm dev --filter api`). Every request stores what the next one needs, so
the folders below are an ordered flow rather than a menu:

1. **Health** — liveness and readiness (ADR-0016).
2. **Admin Auth** — the seeded super admin logs in, reads `me`, rotates its
   refresh token twice and proves the rotated-out token is dead (ADR-0018).
3. **Admin › Staff** and **Admin › Users** — the list machinery (pagination,
   sort, filters — ADR-0014) and the create/read/update/revoke flow.
4. **Admin › Role guards** — the same endpoints as a manager and an editor,
   which is where `403` lives (ADR-0019).
5. **User Auth**, **User › Profile**, **Public** — the second population.
6. **Errors & routing** — the envelope's failure branch (ADR-0012, ADR-0013).
7. **Teardown** — logs every session out and clears the tokens.

A collection-level test asserts the envelope on *every* response, so each
request below only states what is specific to it.

The run creates one staff account, one user account and one self-registered
user, each with a timestamped address, and leaves them behind — v1 has no
delete endpoint. `pnpm db:reset` clears them.

Rate limits (ADR-0020) bound how often the whole collection can run against
one API process: it spends 1 of the 5 failed refreshes per 15 minutes, and
~60 of the 300 global requests. Roughly five runs per window.

exec: // Envelope conformance, asserted on every response in the run (ADR-0012).
// Individual requests state only what is specific to them; the two invariants
// below hold for all of them, and a new request inherits them for free.
// `GET /metrics` is the one response in this API that is not the envelope
// (ADR-0066 §2, the delta on ADR-0012): a Prometheus exposition is a wire
// format a scraper defined, and wrapping it would make it unparseable by
// every client that exists. Its own request asserts its shape; the no-store
// invariant below still applies to it.
pm.test("envelope: the response has the documented shape", function () {
// The same id the response header carries, so an operator handed a failing
// response can find the log line from either half of it (ADR-0010).
pm.expect(body, "success and error are mutually exclusive").to.not.have.property("data");
pm.expect(status, "an error envelope never rides a 2xx").to.be.at.least(400);
pm.test("no successful response in this deliverable is cacheable", function () {
// Every route in the first deliverable either issues a credential, consumes
// one, or returns personal data, so every router mounts `noStore`
// (ADR-0020). Failures are excluded because an unmatched path never reaches
// a router. If this ever fails, the question to answer is whether the new
// endpoint really is safe to cache — not whether to delete the assertion.

item.name: Admin Auth
item.description: `/api/v1/admin/auth/*` (ADR-0018). Login and refresh are unauthenticated by definition; `me` is not. The refresh requests below rotate twice on purpose — see 'A rotated-out refresh token is dead'.

exec: pm.test("200 with a CSRF token", function () {
// 32 bytes of CSPRNG output as unpadded base64url. Asserting the shape
// is what would notice a token that stopped being unguessable.
pm.expect(Object.keys(body.data), "the resource is only the token").to.eql(["csrfToken"]);
pm.test("the cookie carries the same value", function () {
// *Every* Set-Cookie, not `headers.get`, which returns only the first:
// the "the other population is untouched" assertion below would otherwise
// read as "the whole response is clean" while inspecting one header.
// One cookie per population since ADR-0056: this segment writes its own
// name and never the other app’s, which is what stops two SPAs against
// one API host stranding each other’s tokens.
pm.expect(header, "readable by the client, which is the mechanism").to.not.include("HttpOnly");
// The load-bearing property: an app on a different host than the API can
// never read the cookie, so the body copy has to be the same value.
// A cached body would hand back a token whose Set-Cookie never arrived.

request.description:
The bootstrap of ADR-0030, and the first request a browser app makes. It is deliberately unauthenticated — it runs at the moment a reloaded page holds no access token, so requiring one would make it uncallable — and it sets or rotates **this segment's own** CSRF cookie — `__Host-machxi.csrf.admin` on `/admin`, `__Host-machxi.csrf.user` on `/user` (ADR-0056, superseding ADR-0029 on that name alone) — while returning the same value in the body. Two copies for two deployments: a same-host app reads the cookie back, and an app on `admin.example.com` against `api.example.com` can only ever see the body.

Nothing below depends on it. This collection runs on `body` transport, where the CSRF check does not apply at all (ADR-0029 §CSRF), so this request documents and asserts the endpoint rather than feeding anything. Both cookies stay at `Path=/` and keep the `__Host-` prefix, but each segment reads and writes only its own: a browser signed into the admin panel and the customer app at once holds two, and neither app's rotation strands the other's token (D12's finding 6).

request.description: Every refresh rotates: the presented token becomes the session's *previous* token and a new pair is issued. The response carries the principal too, so a client restoring a session from storage needs one call rather than a refresh followed by `me`.

exec: pm.test("200 and a rotated pair", function () {

request.description: The second rotation is what makes the next request deterministic: after it, the token the login issued is neither the session's current nor its previous one, so it is simply unknown — no dependence on `REFRESH_ROTATION_GRACE_SEC` having elapsed.

item.name: A rotated-out refresh token is dead

request.description:
Presents the token the login issued, two rotations ago. Note what this is *not*: replaying the immediately previous token inside `REFRESH_ROTATION_GRACE_SEC` is a legitimate retry and answers `200`, and outside that window it answers `AUTH_REFRESH_REUSED` and revokes the session (ADR-0018 §Refresh). This token predates both, so it is `AUTH_INVALID_REFRESH_TOKEN` whenever you run it.

This is the run's one deliberate failed refresh, and the refresh limiter counts only those — 5 per 15 minutes per IP (ADR-0020).

An unknown email and a wrong password are deliberately indistinguishable — same code, same status, same timing, because the service hashes a dummy when no account matches (ADR-0018 §Login). Using an address that exists in no table keeps the seeded admin's login budget for the next run.

exec: pm.test("400 VALIDATION_ERROR naming the field", function () {

request.description: Validation runs before any credential comparison, and `details` carries the field path the client itself used (ADR-0013). The password is only bounded here, never held to the policy — a policy check would answer 'too short to be one of ours' before checking anything.
No credentials at all is `UNAUTHENTICATED`; credentials that fail to verify are `AUTH_TOKEN_INVALID` (next request). Both are 401 — the codes differ because the client's next move does.

pm.expect(pm.response.headers.has("Set-Cookie"), "the link proves a mailbox, not this device").to.be.false;

request.description: Recovery, the half a collection can walk (ADR-0071 §4). The link itself arrives somewhere newman cannot read, so what is proved here is everything either side of it: the answer is `202` with no session and no cookie, and it is the same `202` whether or not an account is behind the address. Walking an actual reset link is the browser tier's, which reads it out of Mailpit.

request.description: One indistinguishable `401` for every way a reset link can fail — unknown, already spent, expired, or minted for the other population (ADR-0071 §4). request.description: Profile, roles and status in one endpoint; email is absent by design, because changing the identifier a session was established with is its own flow. A change to the *role set* revokes that account's sessions in the same transaction — `authorize` reads roles from the token's claims, so a demotion that left the old token alive would be reversible by its own subject (ADR-0019, amended step 9).

A sub-resource rather than a field of the staff member: ending somebody else's sessions is an action with a side effect, and `POST` is what says so. `204` — the sessions are gone and there is nothing to say about them.

`currentPassword` here is the **caller's own**, not the subject's (ADR-0027 rule 1): the id in the path says whose password is being set, and the body says who is asking. Without it, a stolen admin access token would be enough to take over every operator it outranks.

A sub-resource rather than a field on `PATCH /:id`, so no request exists that can rotate a credential while editing a name. Every session of the subject ends, with no exception — the 'Admin › Profile' folder logs in with the new password, which is what proves this landed.

request.description: `403`, not `401`: the caller's session is valid and stays valid. The same code answers all four credential endpoints of both populations, which is why it is `AUTH_`-prefixed rather than named after a module.

request.description:
`POST /admin/staff/:id/email` (ADR-0071 §7) — the one route under `/admin/staff` that narrows the mount's `admin` guard to `super_admin`. This run is signed in as the seeded super admin, so it passes; the refusal of a plain `admin` is proved in `staff-admin.int.test.ts`, because this collection has no plain-admin fixture to send it with.

`currentPassword` is the **caller's own**, as on the password reset beside it: setting an address redirects every future recovery link, so a stolen access token must not be enough on its own. Nothing is mailed and nothing is confirmed — the operator is the authority a confirmation link would be asking.

pm.expect(staff.status, "no password in the body means an invitation").to.eql(

request.description:
The same endpoint with the `password` **omitted** (ADR-0071 §8): the row is created `invited` with a null hash and an onboarding link is mailed to the address, so the operator chooses their own credential and it never travels through whoever created the row.

There is no `status` field for the body to disagree with — which of the two accounts this makes is decided by whether a credential was supplied. The `locale` rides along because an invited row has no stored one to write the message in (§2).

The address is timestamped so the run is repeatable, exactly as the request above.

A fresh link for an operator who has not accepted the first one (ADR-0071 §8). The mint supersedes the live token for the pair (§1), so pressing this five times leaves one working link rather than five — and the previous one stops working, which is the property that makes offering "resend" safe.

No address in the body and no credential: the message goes to the address **on the row**, so nothing a caller sends can redirect it, and the `admin` mount is the whole guard. Whether the link itself works is the browser tier's to prove, because only a tier that can read the mailbox can follow one.

item.name: Re-send it to somebody who has already joined

request.description:
`409` and not a silent `204` (ADR-0071 §8): the account exists and the caller may read it, and what refuses is the row's **state** — an operator who has already chosen a password has no pending invitation to replace, and a `disabled` one must not be handed a way back in by mail.

It names the conflict because only an authenticated `admin` reaches it, and they can already read the status they are being told about (ADR-0020 §Enumeration).

item.name: Set a password for the invited operator

request.description:
The invitation is how an operator gets their **first** password (ADR-0071 §8, amended at `D18.11`). Writing one here would leave `status` at `invited`, so the credential handed over could not be used — login refuses every inactive row — and the `204` would be a claim nobody could act on.

`409` rather than `403`: the caller has the privilege and what refuses is the row's state, which is `STAFF_LAST_SUPER_ADMIN`'s reason exactly.

item.name: Activate the invited operator by hand

request.description:
The same row from the other direction. `status` is an ordinary field of `updateStaffBody`, so without this refusal an admin could patch an invitation to `active` and produce an operator who can never sign in — and whom the last-super-admin count treats as a survivor, because that query reads `status` alone (ADR-0071 §8, amended at `D18.11`).

What is refused is the **pairing** rather than the transition: every other status still moves, and the request below puts this row somewhere else and back.

item.name: Get a staff member that does not exist

request.description: A well-formed id that no row holds. The caller is an authenticated admin, so `404` discloses nothing they could not learn from the list endpoint.

request.description: Emails are unique within a population, and this endpoint may name the conflict because its caller is authenticated staff. Public self-registration must not — see 'Register the same address again' (ADR-0020 §Enumeration).

pm.expect(body.meta.pagination.total, "the aggregate was skipped, not zeroed").to.eql(null);

request.description:
`count=false` skips the `COUNT(*)` and answers `total: null` — the branch the envelope has always allowed and `GridPager` has always had (ADR-0060 §2). The default stays `true`: an admin grid wants its page count, and only the call site that has become expensive knows it has.

The control is "List users" three requests up, which sends no flag and asserts `total` is a number; a `pm.sendRequest` control inside a `pm.test` here would be scored as a pass unconditionally, for the reason "Update my profile with an email" records.

item.name: List users — an offset past the ceiling is refused

request.description:
`offset` is capped at 10 000 (ADR-0060 §1). Beyond it the answer is the ordinary `VALIDATION_ERROR` — the same shape `?limit=101` gets — rather than a query Postgres serves by walking the table. The successor for a list that must page deeper is keyset pagination, which ADR-0060 names and deliberately does not build.

That the ceiling *itself* is legal is asserted by the integration tier (`list-query.int.test.ts`, "allows the ceiling itself"), where a second request costs nothing and is really checked.

item.name: Admin › Profile
item.description:
`/api/v1/admin/profile` — the staff mirror of `/api/v1/user/profile` (ADR-0027).

Until D2.3 a staff password was written once, at creation, and never again: an operator could not change it and nobody could reset it. This folder acts as the staff account 'Admin › Staff' created and whose password 'Admin › Staff' then reset, never as a seeded fixture, so the run stays repeatable.

request.description:
The bootstrap of ADR-0030, and the first request a browser app makes. It is deliberately unauthenticated — it runs at the moment a reloaded page holds no access token, so requiring one would make it uncallable — and it sets or rotates **this segment's own** CSRF cookie — `__Host-machxi.csrf.admin` on `/admin`, `__Host-machxi.csrf.user` on `/user` (ADR-0056, superseding ADR-0029 on that name alone) — while returning the same value in the body. Two copies for two deployments: a same-host app reads the cookie back, and an app on `admin.example.com` against `api.example.com` can only ever see the body.

Nothing below depends on it. This collection runs on `body` transport, where the CSRF check does not apply at all (ADR-0029 §CSRF), so this request documents and asserts the endpoint rather than feeding anything. Both cookies stay at `Path=/` and keep the `__Host-` prefix, but each segment reads and writes only its own: a browser signed into the admin panel and the customer app at once holds two, and neither app's rotation strands the other's token (D12's finding 6).

item.name: Teardown
item.description:
Leaves the database as the run found it.

Until D2.4 this folder *disabled* the three accounts each run creates, because v1 had no delete endpoint — a live account with a password committed in this repository is a way in, and a disabled one is a row (ADR-0021, D1.10 amendment). It can now delete them, which is neither, and ADR-0028 §Consequences is where that change is recorded: the collection changes, the frozen ADR does not.

The deletes double as the documentation of all three endpoints, including the asymmetry between them — a deleted staff row is gone, a deleted user row is still readable and no longer writable, and since D12.4 a customer can close their own account without an operator, which ends every session including the one that asked.

item.name: Log the created user out everywhere

request.description: `logout` ends the calling session; `logout-all` ends every session the principal holds. Both answer `204`.

item.name: The created user's token is dead

request.description: The access token still verifies — it is signed and unexpired — but its session row is revoked, and `authenticate` checks the session on every request. That is the difference between `AUTH_TOKEN_INVALID` and `AUTH_SESSION_REVOKED`.

item.name: Delete the staff account this run created

request.description:
A **hard** delete: the row goes and `staff_roles` cascades with it (ADR-0028). Staff have no `deleted_at` — a staff member is a directory entry, where a customer record is referenced by future order history.

The caller is the seeded super admin, which matters for the two rules a guard cannot express: nobody deletes themselves, and only a super admin may delete one.

The other row this run created under `/admin/staff` (ADR-0071 §8), removed for the reason the one above it is: staff addresses are unique with no soft delete, so a run that left its rows behind would grow the directory by two every time it is run.

The token rows go with it — `account_tokens.principal_id` is swept by `db:sessions:prune` once they are consumed or expired (ADR-0071 §1), which is a job rather than a cascade.

item.name: The deleted staff member is gone

request.description: The other half of the asymmetry: where a deleted user still answers `200`, a deleted staff member answers `404`, because the row is not there to read.

item.name: Sign in again as the created account

request.description: The account that closes itself has to be signed in as itself (D12.4), and the logout-all above ended every session it had.

item.name: Close my own account with the wrong password

request.description: The current password is required wherever an account acts on its own credentials or existence (ADR-0027 rule 1), and a wrong one is `403` rather than `401`: the session is fine and stays fine.

item.name: Close my own account, so the run leaves nothing behind

request.description: Self-service closure — the same soft delete `DELETE /admin/users/:id` performs, so everything below about a deleted account holds whichever path closed it (ADR-0028).

item.name: The closed account is signed out everywhere

request.description: Closing an account revokes its sessions in the same transaction, so the token it was holding a moment ago is already dead.

item.name: The deleted user is still readable

request.description: `200`, on purpose: an admin who can list deleted accounts must be able to open one, and answering `404` for a row they were just shown is the worse lie. `status` is written alongside `deleted_at` so that `status` stays truthful on its own — an active-and-deleted account would satisfy `filter[status][eq]=active`.

item.name: A write to the deleted user is refused

request.description:
The read path keeps its tolerance and the write path drops it. Without this, a `PATCH` could set a deleted account back to `active` without clearing `deleted_at` — a row simultaneously active and deleted, which no reader is written to expect.

`409` and not `404`: the account exists and the caller may see it; the request conflicts with its state. `410 Gone` would claim the resource is permanently unavailable at this URL, and it is not.

request.description: Deleting the self-registered account sets up the request below, which is the point of the whole partial-index change.

Two rows now share the address, at most one of them live, which every existing read already tolerates: `findByEmail` filters `deleted_at is null` and is the only lookup authentication uses.
